summary: Suggests a way to use the GeneralText body part of X.400 so that implementations treat text in extended character sets more consistently. It was a standards-track specification. It is now historic.

plainLanguage.summary: Letters from many alphabets need to look right on every computer. This memo suggests one common way to label and send such text.

questions: how to use generaltext in x.400
subtitle: How to send text in many alphabets and scripts through X.400 email

tldr.problem: X.400 email systems needed a standard way to send text in many alphabets (Latin, Greek, Cyrillic, Arabic, Hebrew) so receivers would display them correctly and consistently.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 1502 recommends using the GeneralText body part with ISO 2022 character set switching, keeping US-ASCII as the base and designating other character sets to specific code regions that are invoked for non-ASCII text.
tldr.outcome: This provided a path for international email before Unicode became dominant, but GeneralText was complex and few systems implemented all its levels.

today: RFC 1502 is now historic. X.400 email itself faded as the Internet email (SMTP/MIME) became dominant. MIME and later Unicode/UTF-8 provided simpler solutions for international text that did not require the complexity of ISO 2022 character set switching.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
By 1993, both X.400 email and the Internet had solutions for multiple character sets. X.400 had the GeneralText body part defined in ISO/IEC 10021-7, which could carry different character sets in a single message by using ISO 2022 character set switching. The Internet had MIME, which offered a different approach. RFC 1502 defines a recommended method for using GeneralText consistently so that different implementations handle international text in compatible ways.

The goal is to define a standard way to send European languages in the short term, extend to Hebrew and Arabic in the medium term, and eventually support the full ISO 10646 universal character set. The document provides guidelines both for generating GeneralText messages and for rendering them on systems that may not support all character sets.
sections.plainLanguage: X.400 is an old way to send email. It can carry text in many different alphabets, but every program did it differently. This memo says here is one common way, so everyone talks the same.

sections.title: Character Set Families
sections.content:
The RFC describes three main families of character sets available for X.400. ISO 6937 is a Latin character set with diacritical marks used in Teletex and X.500, but it uses a two-mode encoding (some characters are one byte, others are two) which makes processing complex and cannot easily extend to other languages like Korean or Chinese.

ISO 8859 defines a series of single-byte character sets, each suitable for specific language groups. There are sets for Western European (Latin-1), Central and Eastern European (Latin-2), Cyrillic, Arabic, Hebrew, Greek, and others. All include US-ASCII as a subset and use 8 bits per character. This makes them simpler than ISO 6937, though they do not support mixing multiple non-ASCII alphabets without character set switching.

ISO 10646 is a universal 32-bit character set that eventually includes all used characters. However, at the time of writing it could not be used directly because it violates ISO 2022 rules; various encoding methods are being registered for it.
sections.plainLanguage: There are different ways to number letters. Old Teletex uses weird two-byte codes. ISO 8859 has separate alphabets, one for each language. ISO 10646 is one huge alphabet with room for everything but is hard to send on old systems.

sections.title: Using GeneralText in X.400
sections.content:
GeneralText is an Extended body part in X.400/88 that can carry any ISO-registered character set with proper announcement. It uses ISO 2022 character set switching, which maintains four graphic character sets (G0, G1, G2, G3) and two control character sets (C0, C1) at any time. The message always starts with IA5 (US-ASCII) as the G0 set, and other sets can be designated and invoked through escape sequences.

The RFC recommends that G0 always be US-ASCII (ISO-IR-6), designated by the escape sequence ESC 2/8 4/2 at the start of the message. For text representable in one ISO 8859 set, the G1 set should be designated to that set (e.g., ESC 2D 41 for ISO 8859-1, West European). The selected character sets are listed in the message parameters so that receiving systems know what to expect.
sections.plainLanguage: GeneralText says: start with English, then announce when you switch to another alphabet. Every program sees the announcement and knows to switch how it reads the bytes.

sections.title: Recommendations for Encoding
sections.content:
The RFC provides specific encoding guidelines for different scenarios. When text is representable in ISO 8859, keep US-ASCII as G0 and set G1 to the appropriate ISO 8859 part. If text uses multiple non-Latin scripts (Greek, Cyrillic, Hebrew, Arabic), designate the main script as G1 and permanently shift it into the upper half of the code page, while keeping G0 as US-ASCII. Occasional extensions using accents or national variants can be designated to G2 and invoked with single shift sequences.

For Japanese text, the RFC notes that the Japanese community uses a different technique, switching between ISO-IR-87 (Japanese JIS C6226-1983) and US-ASCII as the G0 set. The document also recommends specific sets for multibyte character sets like Japanese, Korean, and Chinese. It warns against using ISO 6937 if other character sets are available, and against using ISO 8859-3 and 8859-4 unless necessary.
sections.plainLanguage: If you are writing in one alphabet, put it in one area. If you use English plus Greek, keep English in the standard area and Greek in the accent area. Always announce before you switch.

sections.title: Guidelines for Rendering GeneralText
sections.content:
Systems that receive GeneralText messages must be able to identify and render characters in IA5 (US-ASCII) regardless of how they are designated or invoked, since these characters are always present. They should always be able to identify their own native character sets and indicate when characters cannot be rendered on the current device. Systems must never render an unknown character by displaying the byte at the same position in the native character set, as this produces incorrect results.

Good implementations can combine floating accents from ISO 6937 with base characters for proper rendering, and can save GeneralText messages preserving all character set information for later processing. The same rendering requirements apply to gateways that transform messages into other formats like MIME.
sections.plainLanguage: A computer reading the message needs to know: can I show this letter? If not, say 'cannot display' rather than guessing. Always read the switching codes before deciding what each byte means.
